text: A ticket is durable, but it isn't where your team is already looking at 2 a.m. — chat is. There are two different jobs chat can do here. Notification just posts a formatted message so a human sees it immediately. ChatOps goes further: it puts an actual Approve or Dismiss button in that message, and clicking it triggers your automation directly. Notification only needs to push a message out; ChatOps needs a channel back in, because the platform has to tell your code which button got clicked.

Teams' simplest path is a push-only incoming webhook: you POST a JSON Adaptive Card to a per-channel URL and Teams renders it, no bot registration required. Slack's equivalent format is Block Kit, and it can render real interactive buttons the same way. But rendering a button and receiving its click are two different problems — the click only reaches your code through a registered Slack app with an interactivity endpoint configured, which is the same receiver shape you already built in Lesson 17.

A Slack message built from Block Kit sections and an actions block will display an Approve button and a Dismiss button right next to the alert text, each carrying the alert's event_id as its value. That part works through a plain incoming webhook, same as Teams. What a plain webhook cannot do is tell your automation that someone actually pressed one — for that, Slack needs an app with interactivity configured, posting the click to an endpoint you control.

That endpoint has to verify every incoming click before trusting it, using Slack's signing secret. The recipe hashes a version tag, a timestamp, and the raw body together, and checking that timestamp first — rejecting anything older than five minutes — blocks a captured request from being replayed later. Only once that signature check passes should the handler read which action_id was clicked and which alert's event_id it belongs to.

Only after verification passes should the handler actually call the ticket functions from the last lesson — escalating or dismissing the case tied to that event_id. The approval button is cosmetic until the request behind it is verified, exactly the same lesson as webhook signatures, now applied to a click. Next lesson ties every piece in this chapter together: making each of these steps safe to retry without doubling up on real-world side effects.
